title: The Dead Sea's shore is the lowest land on Earth, and it drops about a metre a year
body: The Dead Sea, between Jordan, Israel and the West Bank, lies more than **430 m below sea level**, and its shores are the lowest land on Earth. In 1930 its surface stood 390 m below sea level; by 2016 it had fallen to 430.5 m, and the level keeps dropping by more than a metre a year, largely because water that once flowed in from the River Jordan is diverted upstream. The water is about 34% salt, roughly 9.6 times saltier than the ocean, so dense that a person simply floats, and so harsh that no fish or aquatic plants survive in it, only microbes.

slides.alt: A stone marker at the Dead Sea reading 'World's lowest point, 394 metres below sea level', photographed in 1971
slides.caption: A roadside marker in 1971 gave the shore as 394 m below sea level. The surface has since fallen by more than 40 m.

Salt content, relative to the ocean
slides.note: 34.2% salinity measured in 2011, about 9.6 times seawater

slides.question: How salty is the Dead Sea, by weight?
slides.explanation: 34.2% in 2011, about 9.6 times the ocean. The water's density of around 1.24 kg per litre is higher than a human body's, so swimmers float without trying.

slides.question: Why is it called the Dead Sea?
options: Its salt keeps out fish and water plants
Ships sink in its heavy water
slides.explanation: The extreme salinity keeps out fish and aquatic plants; only tiny amounts of bacteria and microbial fungi live in it. People, by contrast, float easily.

slides.label: how much the surface drops each year
slides.text: The level has fallen from 390 m below sea level in 1930 to more than 430 m today, largely because water that once reached it from the River Jordan is diverted upstream.
